standing_assumptions: Setting. The work is a textbook: Aronow and Miller, Foundations of Agnostic Statistics (Cambridge University Press, 2019). Every statement is about random variables on a probability space; Part II adds i.i.d. sampling; Part III adds the missing-data and potential-outcomes models. Locations give the printed page and the one-based page of main.pdf (316 pp.; in the body, PDF page = printed page + 18). Statements were transcribed from the page images (the 110 dpi staged renders, with higher-resolution renders of the same PDF pages where subscripts were small) and compared with the text layer for wording. (S1) Probability space. [Definition 1.1.1, p. 6 (PDF p. 24)] A set $S$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is an event space if it satisfies the following: Nonempty: $S \ne \emptyset$. Closed under complements: if $A \in S$, then $A^C \in S$. Closed under countable unions: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$, then $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ... \in S$. [Definition 1.1.2, p. 7 (PDF p. 25)] Kolmogorov Axioms. Let $\Omega$ be a sample space, $S$ be an event space, and $P$ be a probability measure. Then $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space if it satisfies the following: Non-negativity: $\forall A \in S$, $P(A) \ge 0$, where $P(A)$ is finite and real. Unitarity: $P(\Omega) = 1$. Countable additivity: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$ are pairwise disjoint, then $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) + ... = \sum_i P(A_i)$. [Footnote 11, p. 8 (PDF p. 26)] This assumption [that $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space] shall henceforth be implicit in all definitions and theorems referring to $\Omega$, $S$, and/or $P$. (S2) Random variables and their distributions. [Definition 1.2.1, p. 16 (PDF p. 34)] A random variable is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, $\forall r \in \mathbb{R}$, $\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le r\} \in S$. [Definition 1.2.2, p. 16] Let $g : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function, where $X(\Omega) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then, if $g \circ X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a random variable, we say that $g$ is a function of $X$, and write $g(X)$ to denote the random variable $g \circ X$. [p. 17 (PDF p. 35)] we use $\Pr[\cdot]$ to denote the probability that some condition(s) on a random variable will hold, or, equivalently, the probability that the event defined by those conditions will occur. [Definition 1.2.4, p. 18 (PDF p. 36)] A random variable $X$ is discrete if its range, $X(\Omega)$, is a countable set. [Definition 1.2.5, p. 18] For a discrete random variable $X$, the probability mass function of $X$ is $f(x) = \Pr[X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.11, p. 21 (PDF p. 39)] For a random variable $X$, the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.14, p. 24 (PDF p. 42)] A random variable $X$ is continuous if there exists a non-negative function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the CDF of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x] = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)du$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is called the probability density function (PDF). [Definition 1.2.15, p. 25 (PDF p. 43), as printed; see finding P001-C01-E002] For a continuous random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, the probability density function of $X$ is $f(x) = \left.\frac{dF(u)}{du}\right|_{u=x}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49)] For a random variable $X$ with PMF/PDF $f$, the support of $X$ is $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) > 0\}$. [Definition 1.3.1, p. 31] Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Then $X = Y$ if, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $X(\omega) = Y(\omega)$. [Definition 1.3.16, p. 38 (PDF p. 56)] Let $X$ and $Y$ be either two discrete random variables with joint PMF $f$ or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF $f$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent if, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$. We write $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$. [Definition 1.4.1, p. 39 (PDF p. 57)] A random vector (of length $K$) is a function $\mathbf{X} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^K$ such that, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $\mathbf{X}(\omega) = (X_{[1]}(\omega), X_{[2]}(\omega), ..., X_{[K]}(\omega))$, where $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $X_{[k]}$ is a random variable. (S3) Expectations. [Definition 2.1.1, p. 45 (PDF p. 63)] For a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function (PMF) $f$, if $\sum_x |x|f(x) < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x xf(x)$. For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function (PDF) $f$, if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x|f(x)dx < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x)dx$. [Footnote 2, p. 45] This regularity condition (and the corresponding one in the continuous case) is known as absolute convergence. It is virtually always satisfied in practice, so we omit this technical condition from all subsequent discussion of expectations. [Footnote 3, p. 49 (PDF p. 67)] This theorem, and every subsequent theorem that we only prove for these two cases [two discrete random variables with joint PMF, or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF], also holds when one random variable is discrete and the other continuous. [Definition 2.1.12, p. 52 (PDF p. 70)] The variance of a random variable $X$ is $\mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^2]$. [Definition 2.1.15, p. 53 (PDF p. 71)] The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is $\sigma[X] = \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[X]}$. [Definition 2.1.22, p. 57 (PDF p. 75)] For a random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the mean squared error of $X$ about $c$ is $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$. [Definition 2.2.1, p. 59 (PDF p. 77)] The covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y])]$. [Definition 2.2.5, p. 62 (PDF p. 80)] The correlation of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with $\sigma[X] > 0$ and $\sigma[Y] > 0$ is $\rho[X, Y] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}$. [Definition 2.2.10, p. 67 (PDF p. 85)] For discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \sum_y yf_{Y|X}(y|x)$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. For jointly continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PDF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yf_{Y|X}(y|x)dy$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.12, p. 68 (PDF p. 86)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$, the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{V}[Y|X = x] = \mathrm{E}[(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x])^2|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.15, p. 69 (PDF p. 87)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the conditional expectation function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [p. 70 (PDF p. 88)] We write $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ to denote $G_Y(X)$; the conditional variance function is $H_Y(x) = \mathrm{V}[Y|X = x]$, and $\mathrm{V}[Y|X]$ denotes the random variable $H_Y(X)$. [Footnote 14, p. 70] Ignoring some unimportant measure-theoretic regularity conditions, namely $X(\Omega) = \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. The multivariate versions are Definitions 2.3.3 and 2.3.4 (p. 85, PDF p. 103) and the multivariate BLP, Definition 2.3.6 (p. 86, PDF p. 104; transcribed in the targets that use it). (S4) Sampling and asymptotics. [Definition 3.1.1, p. 92 (PDF p. 110)] Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be random variables with CDFs $F_1, F_2, ..., F_n$, respectively. Let $F_A$ denote the joint CDF of the random variables with indices in the set $A$. Then $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ are independent and identically distributed if they satisfy the following: Mutually independent: $\forall A \subseteq \{1, 2, ..., n\}$, $\forall(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $F_A((x_i)_{i \in A}) = \prod_{i \in A} F_i(x_i)$. Identically distributed: $\forall i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ and $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, $F_i(x) = F_j(x)$. [p. 92] When we have i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, we use the unsubscripted letter $X$ to denote the random variable whose distribution the i.i.d. draws all share. So, for example, $\mathrm{E}[X]$ denotes the expected value common to $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X_1] = \mathrm{E}[X_2] = ... = \mathrm{E}[X_n]$. [Definition 3.2.1, p. 96 (PDF p. 114)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, a sample statistic is a function of $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$: $T_{(n)} = h_{(n)}(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$, where $h_{(n)} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. [Definition 3.2.2, p. 97 (PDF p. 115)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the sample mean is $\overline{X} = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$. [Definition 3.2.6, p. 99 (PDF p. 117)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$ if, $\forall\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| \ge \epsilon] = 0$, or equivalently, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon] = 1$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$. [Definition 3.2.22, p. 108 (PDF p. 126)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables with CDFs $(F_{(1)}, F_{(2)}, F_{(3)}, ...)$, and let $T$ be a random variable with CDF $F$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in distribution to $T$ if, $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous, $\lim_{n \to \infty} F_{(n)}(t) = F(t)$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)] An estimator $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [Definition 3.3.1, p. 116 (PDF p. 134)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the empirical CDF $\hat F$ of $X$ is $\hat F(x) = \overline{\mathrm{I}(X \le x)}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118 (PDF p. 136)] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Definition 3.3.3, p. 118] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with common CDF $F$, the plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$. The 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' (p. 120, PDF p. 138) are not formally defined in the book (footnote 31 names Hadamard differentiability with respect to the Kolmogorov distance and gives no formal definition). (S5) Regression. [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165), with the plus sign before the last term supplied] For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$, the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression estimator is the function $\hat g(\mathbf{X}) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]}$ such that $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K) = \arg\min_{(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$. We refer to $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as the OLS coefficient estimator. [Definition 4.1.3, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ is the $n \times (K + 1)$ matrix whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row is $(1, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, \cdots, X_{[K]i})$. (S6) Parametric models. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$, and for i.i.d. observations $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. (S7) Missing data. [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Footnote 2, p. 208] Since we are assuming i.i.d. sampling, our inferences do not depend on the unit subscript $i$. [Definition 6.1.5, p. 213 (PDF p. 231)] $Y_i$ is missing completely at random if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i$ and $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$. [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] $Y_i$ is missing at random conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$. [Footnote 6, p. 215] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. (S8) Causal inference. [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.9, p. 244 (PDF p. 262)] $D_i$ is randomly assigned if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i$ and $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$. [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. Notes for the formalizer. (a) The book works with PMFs and PDFs and states pointwise conditions ('for all $x$'); for continuous variables these hold only up to null sets (finding P001-C01-E002), so a measure-theoretic formalization should read densities and conditional expectations as versions. (b) Existence and finiteness of the expectations in a statement is a standing convention (footnote 2, p. 45). (c) Asymptotic statements are about an infinite i.i.d. sequence and $n \to \infty$. (d) In a target's statement, text in square brackets is a label or a remark of the transcriber, not the book's words.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The implication drawn from Theorem 2.1.21 and the bivariate normal PDF of footnote 13, corrected
canonical_claim.location: p. 56 (PDF p. 74), Theorem 2.1.21 and the sentence after it; p. 66 (PDF p. 84), footnote 13
canonical_claim.statement: [Theorem 2.1.21, p. 56, as printed; unchanged] Theorem 2.1.21. Properties of the Normal Distribution. Suppose $X \sim N(\mu_X, \sigma_X^2)$ and $Y \sim N(\mu_Y, \sigma_Y^2)$. Then - $\forall a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ne 0$, if $W = aX + b$, then $W \sim N(a\mu_X + b, a^2\sigma_X^2)$. - If $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$ and $Z = X + Y$, then $Z \sim N(\mu_X + \mu_Y, \sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2)$. [Corrected sentence, p. 56] This theorem has an interesting and immediate implication: any nontrivial linear combination of any number of mutually independent normal random variables must itself be normal. [In full] Let $X_1, ..., X_n$ be mutually independent with $X_j \sim N(\mu_j, \sigma_j^2)$, and let $a_1, ..., a_n, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j \ne 0$ for at least one $j$. Then $\sum_{j=1}^{n} a_jX_j + b \sim N\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n} a_j\mu_j + b,\ \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_j^2\sigma_j^2\right)$. [Corrected footnote 13, p. 66] While $\rho[X, Y] = 0$ does not generally imply $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$ even when $X$ and $Y$ are both normal, it does in the special case where the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ is bivariate normal, that is, $X$ and $Y$ have the joint PDF $f(x, y) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_X\sigma_Y\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}}e^{-\frac{1}{2(1 - \rho^2)}\left[\frac{(x - \mu_X)^2}{\sigma_X^2} + \frac{(y - \mu_Y)^2}{\sigma_Y^2} - \frac{2\rho(x - \mu_X)(y - \mu_Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}\right]}$ for some $\mu_X, \mu_Y, \sigma_X, \sigma_Y, \rho \in \mathbb{R}$ with $\sigma_X > 0$, $\sigma_Y > 0$, and $-1 < \rho < 1$. [Formal content of the footnote] For such $f$: (i) $f$ is a joint PDF; (ii) $\mu_X = \mathrm{E}[X]$, $\mu_Y = \mathrm{E}[Y]$, $\sigma_X = \sigma[X]$, $\sigma_Y = \sigma[Y]$, and $\rho = \rho[X, Y]$; (iii) if $\rho = 0$, then $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$ for all $x, y$, so $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$.

[Definition 2.1.19, p. 55 (PDF p. 73)] A continuous random variable $X$ follows a normal distribution if it has PDF $f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, for some constants $\mu, \sigma \in \mathbb{R}$ with $\sigma > 0$; written $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$. [Theorem 2.1.20, p. 56] If $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, then $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mu$ and $\sigma[X] = \sigma$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (confirmed by batch validation): 'any linear combination' includes the all-zero case; the footnote prints $-1 \le \rho \le 1$, $\rho(X, Y)$ for $\rho[X, Y]$ and $\mu_y$ for $\mu_Y$ in the cross term. The corrected implication follows from the two bullets of Theorem 2.1.21 by induction after dropping the terms with $a_j = 0$. The book omits the proof of Theorem 2.1.21.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Figure 2.1.1 (Minimum MSE Solution for a Fair Coin Flip): the vertical scale, corrected; with Theorem 2.1.23 (Alternative Formula for MSE), Theorem 2.1.24 (The Expected Value Minimizes MSE) and Example 2.1.25
canonical_claim.location: Figure 2.1.1: p. 59 (PDF p. 77). Theorem 2.1.23: p. 57 (PDF p. 75). Theorem 2.1.24 and Example 2.1.25: p. 58 (PDF p. 76)
canonical_claim.statement: [Theorem 2.1.23, p. 57, as printed] Alternative Formula for MSE. For a random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2] = \mathrm{V}[X] + (\mathrm{E}[X] - c)^2$. [Theorem 2.1.24, p. 58, as printed] The Expected Value Minimizes MSE. For a random variable $X$, the value of $c$ that minimizes the MSE of $X$ about $c$ is $c = \mathrm{E}[X]$. [Example 2.1.25, p. 58, as printed] A Fair Coin Flip. Let $X = 0$ if the coin comes up heads and $X = 1$ if the coin comes up tails. The PMF of $X$ is $f(x) = \frac{1}{2}$ for $x \in \{0, 1\}$ and $0$ otherwise, so the MSE about $c$ is $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2] = \frac{1}{2}(0 - c)^2 + \frac{1}{2}(1 - c)^2 = \frac{1}{2}(c^2 + 1 + c^2 - 2c) = \frac{1}{2}(1 + 2c^2 - 2c) = \frac{1}{2} + c^2 - c$. The first-order condition is thus $0 = \frac{d}{dc}\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2] = \frac{d}{dc}\left(\frac{1}{2} + c^2 - c\right) = 2c - 1$, which is solved by $c = \frac{1}{2}$. This is $\mathrm{E}[X]$. [Printed figure, p. 59] FIGURE 2.1.1. Minimum MSE Solution for a Fair Coin Flip. Vertical axis labelled MSE with tick labels 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12; horizontal axis 'Choice of c' with tick labels -2, -1, 0, 1, 2. The curve starts at about $(-2, 13)$, has its minimum of about $\frac{1}{2}$ at $c = \frac{1}{2}$ (dashed vertical line) and ends at about $(2, 5)$. [Corrected figure] Relabel the vertical axis $2 \times \mathrm{MSE}$; or keep the label MSE and halve the tick labels to 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (equivalently, plot $c^2 - c + \frac{1}{2}$). The dashed line stays at $c = \frac{1}{2}$. [Formal content] For the fair coin flip $X$ of Example 2.1.25 and $L(c) = \mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$: (i) $L(c) = c^2 - c + \frac{1}{2}$ for all $c \in \mathbb{R}$; (ii) $L(-2) = \frac{13}{2}$, $L(2) = \frac{5}{2}$, and $L(c) \ge L(\frac{1}{2}) = \frac{1}{4} = \mathrm{V}[X]$ with equality only at $c = \frac{1}{2} = \mathrm{E}[X]$; (iii) the plotted values $13$, $\frac{1}{2}$ and $5$ at $c = -2, \frac{1}{2}, 2$ are those of $2L(c) = (0 - c)^2 + (1 - c)^2 = 2c^2 - 2c + 1$, the unweighted sum of the two squared errors.

canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] Theorem 2.2.6. Correlation and Linear Dependence. For random variable $X$ and $Y$, - $\rho[X, Y] \in [-1, 1]$. - $\rho[X, Y] = 1 \iff \exists a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $b > 0$ such that $Y = a + bX$. - $\rho[X, Y] = -1 \iff \exists a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $b > 0$ such that $Y = a - bX$. [What is refuted] The forward implications ($\Rightarrow$) of the second and third bullets, with equality of random variables as in Definition 1.3.1 ($\forall \omega \in \Omega$). The first bullet and both reverse implications are not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validator] Let $\Omega = \{u, v, n\}$, $S = \mathcal{P}(\Omega)$, $P(\{u\}) = P(\{v\}) = \frac{1}{2}$, $P(\{n\}) = 0$. Let $X(u) = 0$, $X(v) = 1$, $X(n) = 0$; $Y_+(u) = 0$, $Y_+(v) = 1$, $Y_+(n) = 1$; $Y_-(u) = 1$, $Y_-(v) = 0$, $Y_-(n) = 0$. Then: (a) each of $X$, $Y_+$, $Y_-$ has mean $\frac{1}{2}$ and variance $\frac{1}{4}$, so the correlations are defined; (b) $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y_+] = \frac{1}{4}$ and $\rho[X, Y_+] = 1$; $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y_-] = -\frac{1}{4}$ and $\rho[X, Y_-] = -1$; (c) if $Y_+ = a + bX$ at every $\omega$, then $u$ gives $a = 0$, $v$ gives $b = 1$, and $n$ gives $1 = a + b \cdot 0 = 0$, a contradiction; so no $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $Y_+ = a + bX$; (d) if $Y_- = a - bX$ at every $\omega$, then $u$ gives $a = 1$, $v$ gives $b = 1$, and $n$ gives $0 = a - b \cdot 0 = 1$, a contradiction; (e) $\Pr[Y_+ = X] = 1$ and $\Pr[Y_- = 1 - X] = 1$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 2.2.21 (Best Linear Predictor) and the first-order conditions in its proof, with the derivatives taken in the free arguments $(a, b)$ and evaluated at $(\alpha, \beta)$; the two corollaries and Theorem 2.2.22
canonical_claim.location: Theorem 2.2.21: p. 76 (PDF p. 94). Proof and footnote 19: pp. 77–78 (PDF pp. 95–96). Corollaries: p. 78 (PDF p. 96). Theorem 2.2.22: p. 79 (PDF p. 97)
canonical_claim.statement: [Theorem 2.2.21, p. 76, as printed; unchanged] Theorem 2.2.21. Best Linear Predictor (BLP). For random variables $X$ and $Y$, if $\mathrm{V}[X] > 0$, then the best (minimum MSE) linear predictor of $Y$ given $X$ is $g(X) = \alpha + \beta X$, where $\alpha = \mathrm{E}[Y] - \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\mathrm{V}[X]}\mathrm{E}[X]$, $\beta = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\mathrm{V}[X]}$. [Footnote 18: If $\mathrm{V}[X] = 0$, then any function such that $g(\mathrm{E}[X]) = \mathrm{E}[Y]$ would minimize MSE. Thus, unlike the CEF, the BLP is not necessarily uniquely defined.] [Printed proof step, p. 77] Let $\varepsilon = Y - (a + bX)$. If $g(X) = \alpha + \beta X$ is the best linear predictor of $Y$ given $X$, then $(\alpha, \beta) = \arg\min_{(a, b) \in \mathbb{R}^2}\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2]$. The first-order conditions yield the system of equations $0 = \frac{\partial\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2]}{\partial\alpha}$, $0 = \frac{\partial\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2]}{\partial\beta}$. ... this becomes: $0 = \frac{\partial\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2]}{\partial\alpha} = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\partial\varepsilon^2}{\partial\alpha}\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[2\varepsilon\frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial\alpha}\right] = -2\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon]$, $0 = \frac{\partial\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon^2]}{\partial\beta} = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{\partial\varepsilon^2}{\partial\beta}\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[2\varepsilon\frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial\beta}\right] = -2\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon X]$. Now we solve $0 = \mathrm{E}[Y - (\alpha + \beta X)]$ and $0 = \mathrm{E}[(Y - (\alpha + \beta X))X]$. [Corrected proof step] Define $Q(a, b) = \mathrm{E}[(Y - a - bX)^2]$. The first-order conditions are $0 = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial a}(\alpha, \beta)$ and $0 = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial b}(\alpha, \beta)$, where $\frac{\partial Q}{\partial a}(a, b) = -2\mathrm{E}[Y - a - bX]$ and $\frac{\partial Q}{\partial b}(a, b) = -2\mathrm{E}[(Y - a - bX)X]$. In footnote 19 the second-order derivatives are $\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial a^2} = 2$, $\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial b^2} = 2\mathrm{E}[X^2]$, $\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial a\partial b} = 2\mathrm{E}[X]$, with $\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial a^2}\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial b^2} - \left(\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial a\partial b}\right)^2 = 4\mathrm{V}[X] > 0$ (the second row of the footnote has scalar $X$ where the page prints one bold $\mathbf{X}$). [Formal content] Let $X$ and $Y$ have finite second moments and $\mathrm{V}[X] > 0$. (i) $Q$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the partial derivatives above. (ii) The system $\mathrm{E}[Y - a - bX] = 0$, $\mathrm{E}[(Y - a - bX)X] = 0$ has the unique solution $b = \beta = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\mathrm{V}[X]}$, $a = \alpha = \mathrm{E}[Y] - \beta\mathrm{E}[X]$. (iii) $Q(a, b) \ge Q(\alpha, \beta)$ for all $(a, b) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, with equality only at $(a, b) = (\alpha, \beta)$. [Corollaries, p. 78, as printed] The BLP is also the best linear approximation of the CEF; setting $a = \alpha$ and $b = \beta$ minimizes $\mathrm{E}[(\mathrm{E}[Y|X] - (a + bX))^2]$. If the CEF is linear, then the CEF is the BLP. [Theorem 2.2.22, p. 79, as printed] Properties of Deviations from the BLP. Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables and let $\varepsilon = Y - g(X)$, where $g(X)$ is the BLP. Then $\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon] = 0$; $\mathrm{E}[X\varepsilon] = 0$; $\mathrm{Cov}[X, \varepsilon] = 0$.

canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] Definition 2.3.1. Covariance Matrix. For a random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, the covariance matrix $\mathrm{V}[\mathbf{X}]$ is a matrix whose $(k, k')^{\mathrm{th}}$ entry is $\mathrm{Cov}[X_{[k]}, X_{[k']}]$, $\forall i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$. That is, $\mathrm{V}[\mathbf{X}]$ is the $K \times K$ matrix with rows $(\mathrm{V}[X_{[1]}], \mathrm{Cov}[X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}], \cdots, \mathrm{Cov}[X_{[1]}, X_{[K]}])$, $(\mathrm{Cov}[X_{[2]}, X_{[1]}], \mathrm{V}[X_{[2]}], \cdots, \mathrm{Cov}[X_{[2]}, X_{[K]}])$, ..., $(\mathrm{Cov}[X_{[K]}, X_{[1]}], \mathrm{Cov}[X_{[K]}, X_{[2]}], \cdots, \mathrm{V}[X_{[K]}])$. [Corrected statement] ... whose $(k, k')^{\mathrm{th}}$ entry is $\mathrm{Cov}[X_{[k]}, X_{[k']}]$, $\forall k, k' \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$. [Statements that depend on the definition, p. 84, as printed] Note that this is a symmetric matrix (because $\mathrm{Cov}[X_{[k]}, X_{[k']}] = \mathrm{Cov}[X_{[k']}, X_{[k]}]$, by Theorem 2.2.4, Properties of Covariance) and the diagonal entries are variances (because $\mathrm{Cov}[X_{[k]}, X_{[k]}] = \mathrm{V}[X_{[k]}]$, again by Theorem 2.2.4). canonical_claim.statement: [Definition 3.2.6, p. 99, as printed; unchanged] Convergence in Probability. Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$ if, $\forall \epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr\left[|T_{(n)} - c| \ge \epsilon\right] = 0$, or equivalently, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr\left[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon\right] = 1$. We write $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$ to denote that $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$. [Printed gloss] More specifically, for any $p \in [0, 1]$ and any $\epsilon > 0$, there is always an $N$ large enough that, for every $n \ge N$, the probability that $T_{(n)}$ will be within $\epsilon$ of $c$ is at least $p$. [Corrected gloss] More specifically, for any $p \in [0, 1)$ and any $\epsilon > 0$, there is always an $N$ large enough that, for every $n \ge N$, the probability that $T_{(n)}$ will be within $\epsilon$ of $c$ is at least $p$. [Formal content] For a sequence of random variables $(T_{(n)})$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$: $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$ if and only if $\forall p \in [0, 1)$, $\forall \epsilon > 0$, $\exists N$, $\forall n \ge N$, $\Pr\left[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon\right] \ge p$. The printed version, with $p = 1$ allowed, requires $\Pr\left[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon\right] = 1$ for all $n \ge N$, which convergence in probability does not imply.

[Proof of Theorem 3.2.9, p. 102] $Z_1, Z_2, ..., Z_n$ are i.i.d. random variables with common PMF $f_Z(z) = \Pr[X \le x]$ for $z = 1$, $\Pr[X > x]$ for $z = 0$, $0$ otherwise. [Theorem 3.2.7, p. 100 (PDF p. 118)] Continuous Mapping Theorem (CMT). Let $(S_{(1)}, S_{(2)}, S_{(3)}, ...)$ and $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be sequences of random variables. [Truncation step for the integrable WLLN, from the validator's derivation] for $M > 0$ split $Z_i = Z_i\mathrm{I}(|Z_i| \le M) + Z_i\mathrm{I}(|Z_i| > M)$; the bounded part has finite variance and Theorem 3.2.5 applies to it for each $n$; the mean of the remainder has $\mathrm{E}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i\mathrm{I}(|Z_i| > M)\right| \le \mathrm{E}[|Z|\mathrm{I}(|Z| > M)]$, which tends to 0 as $M \to \infty$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition 3.2.32 (Consistency of Sampling Variance and Standard Error Estimators) and footnote 23, with the estimator's hat restored in four places

canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] Definition 3.2.32. Consistency of Sampling Variance and Standard Error Estimators. For an estimator $\hat\theta$ such that $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} T$, a sampling variance estimator $\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]$ is consistent if $n\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\theta] \xrightarrow{p} \mathrm{V}[T]$ and a standard error estimator $\sqrt{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]}$ is consistent if $\sqrt{n}\sqrt{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\theta]} \xrightarrow{p} \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[T]}$. [Footnote 23] Note that it is equivalent to define these as $n\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\theta] - \mathrm{V}[T] \xrightarrow{p} 0$ and $\sqrt{n}\sqrt{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\theta]} - \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[T]} \xrightarrow{p} 0$, respectively. [Corrected statement] Definition 3.2.32. For an estimator $\hat\theta$ such that $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} T$, a sampling variance estimator $\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]$ is consistent if $n\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta] \xrightarrow{p} \mathrm{V}[T]$ and a standard error estimator $\sqrt{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]}$ is consistent if $\sqrt{n}\sqrt{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]} \xrightarrow{p} \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[T]}$. [Footnote 23] Note that it is equivalent to define these as $n\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta] - \mathrm{V}[T] \xrightarrow{p} 0$ and $\sqrt{n}\sqrt{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]} - \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[T]} \xrightarrow{p} 0$, respectively. [Statement attached to the definition, p. 114, as printed] Note that, due to the CMT, consistency of the sampling variance estimator implies consistency of the corresponding standard error estimator, and vice versa.

[Theorem 3.2.33, p. 114] Estimating the Sampling Variance of the Sample Mean. For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with finite variance $\mathrm{V}[X] > 0$, let $\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\overline{X}] = \frac{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[X]}{n}$. Then $\mathrm{E}[\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\overline{X}]] = \mathrm{V}[\overline{X}]$ and $n\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\overline{X}] - n\mathrm{V}[\overline{X}] = n\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\overline{X}] - \mathrm{V}[X] \xrightarrow{p} 0$. [Definition 3.2.20, p. 107 (PDF p. 125)] the unbiased sample variance is $\hat{\mathrm{V}}[X] = \frac{n}{n - 1}(\overline{X^2} - \overline{X}^2)$.

The provable content attached to it: (i) for a sequence of non-negative random variables $V_n$ and $v \ge 0$, $V_n \xrightarrow{p} v$ if and only if $\sqrt{V_n} \xrightarrow{p} \sqrt{v}$ (the 'vice versa' sentence, by the CMT with $g(u) = \sqrt{u}$ and $g(u) = u^2$); (ii) $V_n \xrightarrow{p} v$ if and only if $V_n - v \xrightarrow{p} 0$ (footnote 23); (iii) for the sample mean, $n\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\overline{X}] = \hat{\mathrm{V}}[X]$ exactly, for each $n \ge 2$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 3.3.6 (Asymptotic Normality of Plug-In Estimators), as printed, read with footnote 31 and Definition 3.2.28
canonical_claim.location: p. 120 (PDF p. 138), Theorem 3.3.6 and footnote 31. Definition 3.2.28: p. 112 (PDF p. 130)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] Theorem 3.3.6. Asymptotic Normality of Plug-In Estimators. If $T$ is well behaved$^{31}$ at $F$ and $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$, then $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal. [Footnote 31, first two sentences] We say $T$ is well behaved if it is Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the Kolmogorov distance. Formally, the Kolmogorov distance between two distributions $F$ and $G$ is given by the value of the largest divergence between their two CDFs, $\sup_x |F(x) - G(x)|$. [Definition 3.2.28] An estimator $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [What is refuted] The implication for functionals whose Hadamard derivative at $F$ gives a degenerate limit. The implication with a non-degenerate limit is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validator] Let $X_1, X_2, ...$ be i.i.d. Bernoulli($\frac{1}{2}$), with CDF $F$. (a) Let $T_0(G) = 7$ for every CDF $G$. $T_0$ is Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the Kolmogorov (sup) distance, with derivative the zero map. With $\theta = T_0(F) = 7$ and $\hat\theta = T_0(\hat F) = 7$, $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) = 0$ for every $n$; its CDF at 0 equals 1 for every $n$, whereas the CDF of $N(0, \phi^2)$ at 0 is $\frac{1}{2}$ and is continuous at 0, for every finite $\phi > 0$. So $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta)$ does not converge in distribution to $N(0, \phi^2)$ for any finite $\phi > 0$. (b) A non-constant bounded example: $T_1(G) = (G(0) - \frac{1}{2})^2$. Here $F(0) = \frac{1}{2}$, $T_1(F) = 0$, $T_1$ has zero Hadamard derivative at $F$, and $T_1(\hat F) = (\hat F(0) - \frac{1}{2})^2$ with $n\hat F(0) \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n, \frac{1}{2})$; for every $n$, $\mathrm{E}\left[\left(\sqrt{n}(T_1(\hat F) - T_1(F))\right)^2\right] = n\mathrm{E}\left[(\hat F(0) - \tfrac{1}{2})^4\right] = \frac{3n - 2}{16n^2} \to 0$, so $\sqrt{n}(T_1(\hat F) - T_1(F)) \xrightarrow{p} 0$, a degenerate limit.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation). [Hadamard differentiability, as used by the validator; the book gives no formal definition (footnote 31: 'Although we do not provide a formal definition, Wasserman (2006, Ch. 2) provides a lucid discussion')] $T$ is Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the sup distance if there is a continuous linear map $L_F$ on the space of bounded functions with the sup norm such that $\frac{T(F + t_rh_r) - T(F)}{t_r} \to L_F(h)$ whenever $t_r \to 0$, $\|h_r - h\|_\infty \to 0$ and each $F + t_rh_r$ is a CDF.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (a) is exact for each $n$: $\sqrt{n}(T_0(\hat F) - T_0(F)) = 0$. (b) the fourth central moment of $\mathrm{Binomial}(n, \frac{1}{2})$ is $\frac{n(3n - 2)}{16}$, so $\mathrm{E}[(\hat F(0) - \frac{1}{2})^4] = \frac{3n - 2}{16n^3}$ and $n\mathrm{E}[(\hat F(0) - \frac{1}{2})^4] = \frac{3n - 2}{16n^2}$ for every $n \ge 1$; Chebyshev's (Markov's) inequality then gives $\Pr[|\sqrt{n}(T_1(\hat F) - T_1(F))| \ge \epsilon] \le \frac{3n - 2}{16n^2\epsilon^2}$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor: the theorem omits the standard positive-limiting-variance proviso of the delta method. The book gives no formal definition of Hadamard differentiability, so a formalization must fix one; under any standard definition a constant functional is differentiable with zero derivative. The validator did not use the raisers' squared-mean example, which is unbounded.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 3.3.6 (Asymptotic Normality of Plug-In Estimators), corrected with the non-degeneracy condition
canonical_claim.location: p. 120 (PDF p. 138), Theorem 3.3.6 and footnote 31; Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected statement] Theorem 3.3.6. Asymptotic Normality of Plug-In Estimators. If $T$ is well behaved at $F$ (Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the Kolmogorov distance, with derivative $\dot T_F$), $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$, and $0 < \mathrm{Var}[\dot T_F(\mathbb{B}_F)] < \infty$, where $\mathbb{B}_F$ is the Gaussian limit of the empirical-CDF process $\sqrt{n}(\hat F - F)$, then $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal: $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$ with $\theta = T(F)$ and $\phi^2 = \mathrm{Var}[\dot T_F(\mathbb{B}_F)]$. [Alternative form given by the validator] If $T$ is well behaved at $F$ and $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$, then $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} \dot T_F(\mathbb{B}_F)$, a centered Gaussian limit that may be degenerate; positive variance is required in addition for asymptotic normality in the sense of Definition 3.2.28.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation). [Objects in the correction] $X_1, X_2, ...$ i.i.d. with CDF $F$; $\hat F$ the empirical CDF of the first $n$ observations; $\mathbb{B}_F$ the $F$-Brownian bridge, the centered Gaussian process with covariance $\mathrm{Cov}[\mathbb{B}_F(s), \mathbb{B}_F(t)] = F(\min(s, t)) - F(s)F(t)$, to which $\sqrt{n}(\hat F - F)$ converges in distribution in the space of bounded functions with the sup norm (Donsker's theorem); $\dot T_F$ the continuous linear Hadamard derivative of $T$ at $F$, defined on a subspace of bounded functions that contains the sample paths of $\mathbb{B}_F$ with probability one. [Footnote 31, p. 120] We say $T$ is well behaved if it is Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the Kolmogorov distance, $\sup_x |F(x) - G(x)|$. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112] $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: The book omits the proof ('which requires empirical process theory') and cites Wasserman (2006, Theorem 2.27). For a linear functional $T(G) = \int a(x)dG(x)$ with $a$ bounded and of bounded variation, the statement reduces, for each $n$, to the exact identity $\sqrt{n}(T(\hat F) - T(F)) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(a(X_i) - \mathrm{E}[a(X)])$, with variance $\mathrm{V}[a(X)]$, and the CLT (Theorem 3.2.24) applies when $\mathrm{V}[a(X)] > 0$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor. The repair adds a mild regularity condition and leaves the conclusion and Definition 3.2.28 unchanged; Theorems 3.4.2 and 3.4.6 assume asymptotic normality separately. The functional-analytic objects ($\mathbb{B}_F$, $\dot T_F$) are not defined in the book; the definitions given here are the standard ones the validator used. Headline claim P001-ch03-H5 ('when $T$ is well behaved at $F$ the plug-in estimator is asymptotically normal') holds with this proviso. The companion Moderate finding P001-C03-E001 concerns the claim that finite variance makes the mean well behaved.
